body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.
As the campaign ramps up ahead of early voting opening tomorrow, stakeholders and interest groups are also voicing their concerns and hopes for the future.
Both the premier and the opposition leader hit the media circuit today, with Ben Carroll facing some questions over his poor polling.

Carbines reiterates Labor's Free Kinder pledge
As we reported earlier this morning, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson wrote to the government in 2024 asking the government to open the door for gap fees to help kinders cover additional services.

"Once you open the door to putting in gap fee charges, not explaining them, suddenly instead of a free service there's suddenly small print saying: 'if you want to come here, you've got to pay more'," Carbines said."We're saying free kinder is not negotiable under Labor."

"We're saying free kinder is not negotiable under Labor."
Labor's Anthony Carbines does storytime
In one of the most bizarre moments I've seen since we've been running this election blog, government minister Anthony Carbines reads out the AI-generated children's book to a room full of reporters.
"Here comes Jess, that Jess-I-amWith her friend One NationAnd "just a cut" plan," Carbines reads.
He reads the entire book over the next three minutes or so.
He said he didn't have a role in the "artistic preparation" but said it was a "team effort" as to who wrote it.
Labor continues AI-assisted attacks on Coalition
As we reported last week, Labor have been happily using AI to craft attack ads on the Coalition in the lead-up to the election.
Minister for Artificial Intelligence Anthony Carbines has also been happy to provide some of the more theatrical moments on the campaign trail so far.
Today was perhaps the most elaborate yet, as Labor printed out what appears to be an AI-generated faux-Dr Seuss book and schoolroom posters to attack the Coalition on their cuts.
The signs listed various attack topics such as cuts to services and "secret deals with One Nation".
The classroom materials also mocked dumped Liberal candidate Paul Lindemann over an incident where he was found to have yelled at a teenage basketball player while acting as coach.
CFMEU organiser 'pushing like f***' to get bikie job
The Big Build Royal Commission has been shown a series of text messages between Joel Leavitt and CFMEU organiser Jerry McQuaid.
In some of the messages read out, it appears McQuaid is trying to get Leavitt a job on a Big Build project in Cranbourne for Laing O'Rourke.
The attempts start in around November 2020, according to the messages and by January 2021 it had not been successful.
In one message McQuaid writes to Leavitt "the CFMEU is pushing like f***".
Leavitt again appears to dodge questions about what he thinks that means.
Chris Carr SC puts to him that Laing O'Rourke was being difficult in McQuaid's attempts to get him onto their job site.
After highlighting his criminal record and that his own name was associated with some notoriety at the time, Leavitt can't answer why Laing O'Rourke may not have wanted him on their job site.
Biodiversity Council calls for parties to halt nature loss
The Biodiversity Council has laid out its hopes for the 2026 Victorian election, calling on all parties to halt and reverse the decline of the state's environment.
A new report from the council says Melbourne residents have the poorest access to national parks and convervation areas of any capital city.
The Biodiversity Council's Sarah Bekessy called on political parties to take action to save the garden srate.

"The next Victorian government has an opportunity to halt the destruction of nature and start rebuilding, but it will take more than promises. We need proper funding, stronger laws and accountability for delivering results," she said.

The council called on the government to close loopholes on native logging and prevent logging by stealth, which enviromental groups say is still occurring despite a statewide ban enforced two years ago.
It also called for more funding for Parks Victoria, saying staffing at the agency had dropped more than 30 per cent since 2020-21.
Seats in focus: Footscray

Labor has had a firm grip on Footscray since it was recreated as a seat in 1927, with the party winning with more than two-thirds of the two-party-preferred vote at most elections. But these margins conceal some complex contests over the years.

Labor’s primary vote dipped under 50 per cent at the 2010 election and the Greens came within about 200 votes of overtaking the Liberals in second place. This was partly due to the strong flow of preferences from independent Catherine Cumming, who ran in the seat at every election from 2002 to 2014.

Weaker preference flows and less favourable boundaries kept the Greens in third for the next few elections. But population growth pushed Footscray further towards the CBD ahead of the 2022 election. Although the Greens’ primary vote only modestly increased, the Liberals were disadvantaged by the new boundaries and ended up in third. The Victorian Socialists also entered the contest and polled nearly 10 per cent, giving the Greens a sizeable pool of preferences from which to maintain their place in second.
Although the Greens failed to win the seat, they reduced Labor’s margin to just over 4 per cent, by far the lowest in the seat’s modern history.

The Greens have a clear path to winning this seat should the Labor vote continue to decline and they get favourable preference recommendations from other parties. While the former seems plausible heading into this election, the latter is never assured.
Early voting kicks off tomorrow
The Victorian Electoral Commission says a record 210 early voting centres will open tomorrow for the state election.
The VEC said there would be 30 per cent more venues for early voting compared to last election, with about 60 per cent of voters expecting to cast their vote before election day.

"You don't need a reason to vote early in Victorian state elections. Early voting in person is a safe, convenient option if you're travelling or working on election day," Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel said."Anyone can choose to vote early. Visit the VEC website to find your nearest early voting centre."

"Anyone can choose to vote early. Visit the VEC website to find your nearest early voting centre."
Early voting centres will operate from 9 am to 6 pm each day until Friday 27 November, except for Sunday 22 November when all voting centres are closed.

Vision Australia calls for Victorian driverless taxi trial
Vision Australia is calling on the next Victorian government to become the first state in the country to fund an autonomous accessible taxi pilot program.
Under current laws, an automated driving system (ADS) permit is required to operate an automated vehicle in automated mode for testing or development purposes.
But Vision Australia’s Chris Edwards says a dedicated driverless taxi pilot would test the practical benefits for all people who cannot drive and provide evidence to guide future transport planning.
"Whether someone is travelling to work, going to a medical appointment or visiting family and friends, the ability to travel independently is pivotal," said Mr Edwards.

"We can see from the national data that only around half of people with disability are currently able to use all forms of public transport without difficulty, so there is certainly room for improvement.
"As Victorians we want to see how this technology could support and build upon existing transport options for people with low vision or who are blind."
Self-driving robotaxis are already in use internationally on the streets of London, San Francisco and Beijing as rideshare companies expand into driverless transport.
The push for robotaxis comes as part of a package of priorities to improve the state for vision-impaired people for the coming election, which also include:
• funding and supporting a training and employment program in Victoria
• higher penalties for dog attacks on dog guides
• audio announcements on public transport
Seats in focus: Evelyn

Evelyn is one of the oldest electoral districts in the state and has always traditionally favoured the conservative side of politics. Since 1985, Labor has only won the seat once, in the "Brackslide" of 2002, and even then with a very small margin.
Despite this history, the seat has often been closely fought between the major parties, as the boundaries have shifted slightly further down the Maroondah Highway toward Melbourne in recent decades.

Current member Bridget Vallence withstood an almost 7 per cent swing against the Liberals when she succeeded longtime member Christine Fyffe in 2018. In 2022, Labor’s primary vote dropped dramatically and she increased her two-party-preferred margin by a few points.
Key Event
Labor promises millions for AFL club facilities
Lost in the election noise is a promise from Premier Ben Carroll to pump tens of millions of dollars into three AFL clubs facilities - which can be used by the community.
Carroll is promising $25 million for his beloved North Melbourne at Arden St, who he has proudly barracked for over the years.
The promise also includes cash for the Bombers' plans to revamp Windy Hill and the Saints in Moorabbin, with both clubs hoping to finally end their decades-long September woes.
But Libertarian MP David Limbrick says there shouldn't be any cash for the "grifters" in the AFL.
"We should stand up to corporate rent-seekers of all kinds, and the AFL are amongst the worst offenders," Limbrick said.

"Many people in my electorate are struggling with the cost of living. They want more police. They want the roads fixed. Providing facilities for millionaire athletes is not high on their list of priorities.
“Providing community facilities for sport is fine, but I think this excuse is a fig leaf for a really unhealthy relationship between the sport and the big political parties."
Labor attacks Jess Wilson over free kinder

Labor has seized on a January 2024 letter that Opposition Leader Jess Wilson sent to Minister for Children, Lizzie Blandthorn, which argued the "restrictive nature of free kinder" meant quality had been compromised.
All Victorian three- and four-year-olds are entitled to free kindergarten under a program launched in 2023, with the government gradually increasing the hours provided.
In her letter, Wilson said teachers at a kindergarten told her they had been forced to cut back because the funded hours did not cover their service.
In a statement, Blandthorn said the letter showed where the Coalition stood on free kinder.
"It's free kinder under Labor, and fee kinder under the Liberals," Blandthorn said.

The minor parties running in the Victorian election
Labor, Liberal, the Greens and One Nation continue to dominate the news cycle, but there are more than a dozen smaller parties vying for a seat in the Victorian parliament this year.
Some parties have been campaigning for decades, while others have popped up to contest in their first ever election.
Check out our guide to find out what each party stands for and is campaigning on this election:
Key Event
Joel Leavitt confirms bikie links to CFMEU

In today's hearing at the Big Build royal commission, Chris Carr SC has gone through a list of names, asking whether Leavitt knows if they were health and safety representatives on Big Build project and whether they were part of any outlaw motorcycle gang.
Leavitt appears to be dodging some of the questions to begin with but eventually answers.
Of the 12 names mentioned, Leavitt confirms he knows seven plus the brother of an eighth.
All of those had a role with the CFMEU.
And to the best of Leavitt's understanding, all bar one were affiliated with an outlaw bikie gang.
Seats in focus: Euroa

Regional Victorian seats underwent a significant redrawing of boundaries in 2013, particularly north of Melbourne. Euroa was created out of the abolished seats of Benalla, Rodney, and Seymour, with the former seats being Nationals strongholds and the latter a swing seat held by both major parties.

The Nationals have had little trouble winning Euroa since 2014. Its first member was Steph Ryan, a former journalist and adviser to Liberal premier Ted Baillieu, who immediately upon entering parliament was elected deputy leader of the Nationals. Citing a desire for a greater work-life balance, Ryan retired ahead of the 2022 election and was succeeded in Euroa by another former journalist, Annabelle Cleeland.

With Ryan’s retirement, the Liberals once again contested Euroa at the 2022 election. They performed best in Benalla, where they outpolled the Nationals on the primary vote, and in the small towns to the west of Shepparton. Labor attracted the most support in the southern end of the seat and in the town of Heathcote in the west.

Heading into this election the question will be whether Cleeland has established enough local support to hold off a One Nation challenge. Like the surrounding rural seats, Euroa’s population is older and less diverse.
Key Event
Low sensory voting centres now open
Low sensory voting centres have opened their doors this morning to those with neurodivergent or sensory needs.
The pilot program includes more space around booths, adjusted lighting, and staff to help those with non-physical disabilities.
"When you make it work and make it more accessible, it's better for everybody," says David Tonge from Amaze, an autism advocacy agency.
He says there have been conversations with some political parties about not trying to overwhelm people with flyers and messages as they enter voting centres this election.
"Victoria's leading the way in this and I think other states and nationally are going to look," he's told 774 ABC Melbourne.
The booths will available in each electoral district from 10am to 4pm today.

Key Event
Outlaw motorcycle gang member, first RC witness to be called
The first witness to be called this morning at the Big Build royal commission is Joel Leavitt who is a member of the Bandidos, an outlaw motorcycle gang.
He was previously a member of the Rebels for about two years, he tells the commission.

He tells Counsel Assisting Chris Carr SC he is currently unemployed but he has been a member of the CFMEU and that he was a health and safety representative "appointed by the builder" on various sites.
Key Event
Coalition pledges to make multigenerational housing easier

Victorians will find it easier to build or renovate homes with separate kitchens and living spaces, under a Coalition plan to give multi-generational families the flexibility to live under the same roof.

Under the National Construction Code, homes with a second kitchen or self-contained living space upstairs must be classified as an apartment building, triggering major additional safety requirements and costs.
The Coalition has promised to review the building code and regulations to allow homes with extra kitchens to remain classified as a single house.
State and territory governments can override the national code with specific legislation.

"Multigenerational housing is this great opportunity to actually match how Victorians are choosing to live," Shadow Housing Affordability Minister Nicole Werner said."It provides a choice for people to be able to either live with grandparents — whether it's for aging in place or for help with child care — or co-purchase with a sibling or friend."

🎞️: Run for Office: Glen Waverley
In the ABC's Run for Office series, our intrepid suburbs reporter Margaret Paul is running through different Victorian electorates and finding out what matters to voters.
She visited the electorate of Glen Waverley in Melbourne's south-east, where the Suburban Rail Loop, car parking and potholes all features as issues on the minds of voters.
Seats in focus: Eureka

The seats covering Ballarat have shifted substantially at the past two redistributions. Eureka was created from the abolished, but similar, seat of Buninyong, which itself was created from much of the former seat of Ballarat East. All three seats cover parts of Ballarat’s eastern suburbs but Eureka now includes the commuter town of Bacchus Marsh and a swathe of small towns to the south of Ballarat.

The seat’s incumbent member, Michaela Settle, was elected to Buninyong in 2018, succeeding longtime Ballarat East MP Geoff Howard. Settle transferred to Eureka in 2022 and in April this year entered cabinet as agriculture minister.

Electorally, Ballarat and its suburbs have a strong Labor history. But Labor’s margin is weaker in the other towns in the seat. One Nation did not contest this seat in 2022, so this election will be a gauge of the party’s current support in semi-rural areas.
Big Build Royal Commission returns
The Big Build Royal Commission has commenced after taking the day off yesterday to review documents belatedly submitted by the state government.
The documents were originally submitted heavily redacted, which was criticised by the commission.
To start today's hearing, Counsel Assisting Chris Young KC read out a letter from Premier Ben Carroll to his department which called on all government departments to comply with the royal commission.
Following his letter, the documents were resubmitted and lawyers scrambled over the weekend to go through them, which is why yesterday's scheduled hearing did not sit.
Key Event
Jess Wilson hits the airwaves to plug campaign
While the premier discussed his favourite non-alcoholic beers, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson was on Nova 100's Jase, Lauren & Clint to talk about her vision for Victoria.

Wilson emphasised her tough-on-crime approach, following up from yesterday's announcement that the Coalition would introduce anti-stalking laws, including placing stalkers under 24-hour GPS monitoring.
She told Nova 100 that the Coalition would also waste no time strengthening bail laws.

"We recall the parliament this side of Christmas if we are successful in two weeks' time and we bring forward legislation that will see our bail law strengthened, a one-strike rule for bail, so that if you break bail, you will go to jail for 25 serious and violent offences," she said.
Have your say on the Victorian election
We want to know what's shaping your vote in this election and why.
Whether it's the cost of living, housing affordability, crime, regional roads, health care or jobs, let us know in our form below.
You can also ask the election questions you want answered from candidates, parties or the ABC.
All submissions will be reviewed by a journalist, and we may be in touch if we need more information.
Key Event
Ben Carroll starts the day on breakfast TV
Premier Ben Carroll started his day with what could best be described as an awkward appearance on Channel Nine's Today Show.

After some to-and-fro with the hosts, who felt he was dodging their questions over poor polling, Carroll was asked about heavily redacted documents submitted by the Big Build authority to the construction royal commission.
The move prompted a warning last week from commissioner Chris Kourakis to government employees about disclosing all information requested by the commission.
On Today, the premier was forced to defend his response to the redacted documents.

"I'm here to fix and clean up, once and for all, any corruption and wrongdoing. That is why, as soon as I found out I took immediate action," he says."I made it very clear, absolute transparency and accountability. There are to be no redactions and since I stepped in, that has been fixed."
"I'm here to fix and clean up, once and for all, any corruption and wrongdoing. That is why, as soon as I found out I took immediate action," he says.
"I made it very clear, absolute transparency and accountability. There are to be no redactions and since I stepped in, that has been fixed."
With the boring stuff out of the way, the hosts then got into the big questions such as whether the premier prefers craft beer or VB.
For the record, Carroll says he drinks non-alcoholic craft beer.
